By leveraging the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study® sample, the present study addresses previous methodological constraints to clarify cannabis’s potential effect on cognitive development.Methods. Youth (N=4,191) performed neurocognitive tasks during their baseline (age ~10) and Year 6 (age ~16) follow-up assessments. Domains included overall cognitive function (crystallized/fluid), memory, executive functioning, processing speed, reward sensitivity, and language skills. Lifetime, cumulative cannabis use was divided along a median split to account for skewed data, resulting in no, low (≤5 cannabis use occasions; average=1.8), and high use (>5 use occasions; average=256) groups. Initial models (Bonferroni corrected, n=19) compared Year 6 follow-up cognitive performance between groups while controlling for baseline performance, sex, and age. Sensitivity analyses incorporated 1) socioeconomic status (SES), 2) additional substance use, and 3) SES and additional substance use.Results. Cannabis use during early adolescence was significantly related (adj. p<0.05) to worse crystallized cognitive function (β=[-0.23,-0.21]), memory (β=[-0.35,-0.17]), and language skills (β=[-0.26,-0.13]). Cannabis effects remained generally consistent after controlling for SES alone. After controlling for additional substance use, the unique effect of cannabis use was no longer statistically significant.Conclusions. The present study highlights that cannabis likely has an overall negative effect on neurocognitive development; while present over and above SES, this effect may not be substance specific. Future work aims to disentangle the shared effect of these relationships.

item.title: Personalized Network Mapping Reveals State-Trait Dissociation of Frontoparietal Connectivity in Adolescent Depression: A Longitudinal Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Prior research linking resting-state networks (RSNs) to adolescent depression has yielded inconsistent findings, partly because group-average templates poorly capture individual brains; a mismatch that may be especially consequential during adolescence, when RSNs grow increasingly heterogeneous across individuals. Using a personalized analysis pipeline in the longitudinal Characterizing Adolescent Trajectories of Depression cohort (38 depressed adolescents [28 female]; ages 14–18; 181 usable scans; avg. participation: 446.18 days), we derived individualized definitions of three canonical depression-related RSNs. Because longitudinal RSN connectivity may reflect both trait-like vulnerability and state-like symptom fluctuation, we used mixed-effects models to decompose connectivity profiles into both components. FPN connectivity showed a significant state-trait dissociation: chronically elevated connectivity predicted greater average symptom burden, while transient increases predicted momentary relief. These effects were undetectable using group-atlas estimates. We suggest FPN connectivity plays a dual, compensatory role in adolescent depression and demonstrate that personalized definitions can reveal clinically meaningful brain–symptom associations.

item.title: Predictive EEG Signatures of Alzheimer's Disease: A Cross-Validated, Cross-Method Analysis Using ANCOVA Filtering and Sparse Logistic Regression
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) changes how the brain’s electrical activity behaves, and these changes can, in principle, be picked up directly from a resting-state EEG recording without any invasive testing. This study asks a much narrower question: does a small subset of four EEG-derived measurement families, namely signal complexity, spectral power, functional connectivity and network topology, reliably separate individuals with AD from Healthy Controls (HC), and does that separation hold up under strict, leakage-free testing? Using a public dataset of 36 AD and 29 HC subjects, candidate features were selected through permutation-based ANCOVA with false discovery rate correction, controlling for age and gender, and each selected feature was then re-checked using a complementary method (Mann-Whitney U with FDR correction, plus network-based statistics for connectivity), applied to the same subjects, to confirm the finding wasn’t an artifact of the first method’s particular assumptions. Agreement between the two methods was strong for signal complexity (Jaccard = 0.85) and spectral power (Jaccard = 0.87), essentially perfect for two of the four network measures (Jaccard = 1.00), and weaker for connectivity (Jaccard = 0.60, assessed at the level of frequency bands). A sparse logistic regression classifier was then trained using 5-fold cross-validation in which feature selection was independently repeated inside each fold, a design specifically intended to stop information from test subjects leaking into which features get chosen. This classifier reached 78.5% ± 5.8% accuracy at discriminating AD from HC (sensitivity 0.803 ± 0.116, specificity 0.753 ± 0.100, AUC 0.808 ± 0.134). A single spectral power feature was among the two features retained in three of the five folds, more than any other individual feature. Taken together, the results point to a real but modest EEG signature of AD in this dataset, identified using a validation design built specifically so that reported accuracy reflects genuine generalization rather than an artifact of how the features were selected.

item.title: Molecularly distinct neurodegeneration shapes the DOPA-dependent dynamic of large-scale brain connectomics in GBA-associated Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract GBA1-associated Parkinson’s disease (GBA1-PD) is a biologically distinct synucleinopathy associated with glucocerebrosidase deficiency, lysosomal dysfunction, and more extensive cortical neurodegeneration. How these molecular abnormalities shape large-scale cortical network dynamics in vivo remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG functional connectivity and network topology in GBA1-PD and to determine whether GBA1-related molecular pathology is associated with a distinct oscillatory connectome signature and its modulation by dopaminergic treatment. We recorded resting-state EEG in 22 patients with PD (GBA1-PD = 7; LRRK2-PD = 5; sporadic PD = 10) together with 14 age-matched healthy controls. EEG was acquired in OFF and ON dopaminergic states. Functional connectivity was estimated using imaginary coherence (ImCoh) and phase-locking value (PLV) across canonical frequency bands, while network organization was quantified using the graph-theoretical clustering coefficient. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess therapy- and subtype-specific effects. GBA1-PD exhibited a selective increase in gamma-band clustering coefficient in the ON condition (p = 0.044), which was not observed in LRRK2 or sporadic PD. PLV-based analyses highlighted opposite clustering changes in GBA1 and LRRK2 patients. ImCoh analyses further revealed different therapy-related connectivity changes in genetic and sporadic PD across all frequency bands (all p ≤ 0.0035). Compared with healthy controls, PD was associated with widespread disruption of cortico-cortical connectivity. All significant effects were abolished in surrogate-data analyses, supporting their physiological specificity. Resting-state EEG connectomics may reveal genotype-specific network alterations in GBA1-PD and their modulation by dopaminergic treatment, supporting a relationship between genetic background and large-scale brain network dynamics.

item.title: Termination Failure as a Framework for Bipolar Disorder: Candidate Mechanisms and Testable Pharmacological Predictions
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Bioenergetic accounts of bipolar disorder (BD) have been shaped by a persistent observation: resting brain ATP and phosphocreatine often appear near-normal, even in symptomatic patients. Challenge-based work has moved the field beyond static measures, showing that patients fail to sustain ATP under high demand, and has framed the core abnormality as a deficit of capacity. This review re-examines that literature from a control perspective and argues that the capacity to terminate demand-driven energetic upregulation has been largely untested, chiefly because resting and single-challenge designs cannot resolve return kinetics. The argument is developed in three steps. First, we review how neuronal energy supply is matched to demand, giving comparable weight to adenine-nucleotide feedback, mitochondrial calcium signalling, and phosphotransfer buffering, and we note evidence that cytosolic ATP and ATP:ADP are strikingly stable during physiological activity. Second, we set out three candidate implementations of the termination step — mitochondrial Ca² efflux via NCLX, adenine ⁺ nucleotide feedback, and the creatine kinase–phosphocreatine system — and grade the evidence for each, distinguishing findings obtained in BD from those extrapolated from other systems. None has been assayed directly in BD tissue. Third, using a minimal control-loop model, we show that reduced termination capacity alone does not generate cycling; depending on parameters it produces slowed return, latching, persistent elevation, or sustained oscillation. Cycling therefore requires additional conditions, which we state explicitly. We close with pharmacological strategies that would discriminate among the candidates.

item.title: Differential Trajectories of Brain Atrophy in Multiple Sclerosis, MOGAD, and AQP4 + NMOSD: The Role of Disease Activity in MOGAD.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Multiple sclerosis (MS), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease (MOGAD), and aquaporin-4 antibody-positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (AQP4 + NMOSD) are inflammatory demyelinating disorders with distinct mechanisms of tissue injury. MS is characterized by diffuse neurodegeneration, whereas damage in antibody-mediated diseases is considered attack related. In MOGAD, the relationship between disease activity and brain atrophy remains unclear. We aimed to compare longitudinal trajectories of global and regional brain atrophy across MS, MOGAD, and AQP4 + NMOSD and investigate whether atrophy in MOGAD is associated with disease course and lesion dynamics. Methods In this retrospective multicenter Magnetic Resonance Imaging in Multiple Sclerosis (MAGNIMS) study, patients fulfilling the following criteria were enrolled: (1) age 18 years or older, (2) MS/MOGAD/AQP4 + NMOSD diagnosis, (3) ≥2 same-scanner brain MRIs ≥6 months apart and ≥3 months postattack, (4) concurrent Expanded Disability Status Scale, and (5) disease course information. White matter lesions were segmented using the Lesion Segmentation Toolbox. Longitudinal brain volumes were quantified on lesion-filled T1-weighted images using Sequence Adaptive Multimodal SEGmentation (SAMSEG) with a within-subject template approach. In MOGAD, lesion dynamics were classified as stable/new lesions/lesion resolution. Linear mixed-effects models adjusted for age, sex, baseline volume, and center estimated atrophy rates. Results Overall, 489 participants from 15 centers were included (98 MS [mean age 39.79 years, 68.37% female], 72 MOGAD [42.14 years, 66.67%], 41 AQP4 + NMOSD [51.25 years, 87.80%], and 278 healthy controls [42.94 years, 61.87%]). The mean follow-up was MS: 2.44 ± 1.55 years, MOGAD: 2.57 ± 1.85, and AQP4 + NMOSD: 3.22 ± 2.42. Compared with controls, MS showed accelerated global brain atrophy (β = -2.027 cm3 per year, 95% CI -3.430 to -0.623). MOGAD demonstrated white matter volume loss (β = -0.989, 95% CI -1.889 to -0.090) and ventricular enlargement (lateral: β = 0.219, 95% CI 0.089-0.350; third ventricle: β = 0.009, 95% CI 0.003-0.015). AQP4 + NMOSD showed pallidal volume reduction (β = -0.008, 95% CI -0.014 to -0.001). Within MOGAD, relapsing patients (62.5%) exhibited greater third ventricular expansion than MS (β = 0.009, 95% CI 0.001-0.017). MOGAD with new lesions (22.22%) had greater ventricular enlargement than controls (lateral: β = 0.359, 95% CI 0.147-0.572; third ventricle: β = 0.016, 95% CI 0.006-0.025), MS, and AQP4 + NMOSD. Discussion Each inflammatory demyelinating disease exhibits a characteristic pattern of brain atrophy. In MOGAD, neuroaxonal loss seems associated with inflammatory activity and lesion accrual, supporting an event-driven pattern of tissue injury rather than diffuse neurodegeneration. Limitations include small NMOSD sample, heterogeneous follow-up, and potential scanner-related variability.

item.title: Plasticity in Human Brain Language Areas After Stroke: What Can the Right Hemisphere Do?
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Among the most devastating effects stroke can have on the lives of survivors and those around them are language production and comprehension impairments. The most notable of them - often given the joint diagnostic label of "aphasia" despite their heterogeneity and dissociability - are associated with damage to the brain's left hemisphere, which, in large part for this reason, is considered the "language-dominant" hemisphere. However, the right hemisphere's contribution to language should not be underestimated and may in fact be key to understanding the possibilities and limitations of neuroplasticity for supporting language recovery after stroke. Thus, in this review, we focus on the role of the right hemisphere in supporting human language function, in the neurologically healthy brain and after stroke. We discuss the remarkable capability of the right hemisphere to support normal language abilities after a large left-hemisphere stroke early in life, the more limited capacity for right-hemisphere language support after left-hemisphere stroke in adulthood, and potential interactions between typically left-hemisphere dominant "core" language functions with language functions typically thought to be right-hemisphere dominant, such as emotional prosody. We conclude by highlighting gaps in current knowledge and suggesting areas for future research.

item.title: The Pallidothalamic Tract in Functional Neurosurgery: A Systematic Review.
item.description:
Stereotactic and functional neurosurgery
Background The pallidothalamic tract (PTT), formed by convergence of the ansa lenticularis and fasciculus lenticularis at Forel's field H1, is a major basal ganglia efferent pathway and an emerging functional neurosurgical target. No systematic review has previously synthesised outcomes across PTT-targeted interventions. Methods This PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD420251248260). PubMed, OVID, and Web of Science were searched for studies reporting functional neurosurgical outcomes targeting the PTT or Forel's fields. Prospective and retrospective studies, case series, and case reports were eligible. Methodological quality was assessed using design-appropriate risk-of-bias tools. Results Forty studies encompassing 483 patients (1966-2025) were included across five modalities: MR-guided focused ultrasound (n=143), radiofrequency ablation (n=167), deep brain stimulation (n=40), cryogenic lesioning (n=82), and oil-wax injection (n=52). Mean follow-up was 21 months. In Parkinson disease (11 studies; n=135), mean UPDRS-III improvement was 39%, with reductions in dyskinesia (UDysRS 90%) and tremor (75%). In dystonia (12 studies; n=87), BFMDRS and TWSTRS improved by 57% and 47%, respectively. Dual-target strategies, particularly PTT-VIM combinations, showed additive effects, including greater tremor reduction (77%) and improved rigidity. In drug-resistant epilepsy (6 studies; n=157), seizure reduction occurred in 71% and seizure freedom in 33%. Conclusions PTT-targeted interventions yield meaningful motor improvements in Parkinson disease and dystonia, with preliminary evidence supporting additive dual-target benefits. Seizure-reducing effects in refractory epilepsy have been reported. Evidence remains limited by small uncontrolled studies, heterogeneous outcomes, and inconsistent adverse-event reporting. Prospective trials will elucidate the efficacy, safety, and clinical role of the PTT in neurosurgery.

item.title: The effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students: Evidence from ERPs.
item.description:
The British journal of educational psychology
Background In multimedia learning, individuals often need to integrate textual and visual information. The neural mechanisms underlying how consistency between text and pictures affects memory integration remain unclear. Aim To examine the effect of text-picture consistency on memory integration in college students and to determine the processing time at which this effect occurs. Sample Totally 28 Chinese college students (nfemale = 20, nmale = 8; Mage = 21.64 ± 2.30) participated in this experiment. Methods An adapted pictorial demonstration paradigm was employed. Participants sequentially learned two pairs of text-picture stem facts (consistent vs. inconsistent), separated by an interval, followed by a recognition test for stem and integrated facts. Behavioural and event-related potential (ERP) data were recorded simultaneously. Results Under the text-picture consistency condition, college students showed significantly better memory integration performance than under the inconsistency condition (58% vs. 48%). EEG results showed that the text-picture inconsistency condition (i.e., the picture and text within a single stem fact were semantically mismatched) elicited a larger P600 wave (500-800 ms) than the text-picture consistency condition, suggesting that text-picture inconsistency primarily induces conflict and integration difficulties during late cognitive processing. No significant differences were observed in the early N400 component. Conclusion Text-picture consistency facilitates memory integration primarily during late processing, aligning with cognitive theories of multimedia learning. Educationally, it serves as a key quality indicator for multimedia material design. Instructors should prioritize semantic alignment and assess knowledge integration during evaluation.

item.title: The network localization and underlying biological basis of heterogeneous structural and functional brain abnormalities in insomnia disorder.
item.description:
Sleep
Insomnia disorder (ID) has become a prevalent sleep disorder worldwide, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear due to heterogeneous neuroimaging findings and uncertain network localization. We identified brain structural and functional abnormality locations associated with ID from 63 published neuroimaging studies, including 3391 patients and 3433 healthy controls. Using coordinate network mapping combined with a normative connectome database, we mapped these abnormalities to large-scale brain networks of ID across imaging modalities and further decoded them by integrating microscale chemo-architectural, cellular, and cognitive maps. The structural network widely involved the ventral attention (VAN), sensorimotor (SMN), dorsal attention (DAN) and default mode network (DMN); the task-induced network showed a similar but less extensive pattern, predominantly implicating the VAN, DMN, SMN and subcortical network (SCN); in contrast, the resting-state network was largely confined to the left middle frontal gyrus and the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex. Molecular mapping revealed both shared and distinct neurotransmitter signatures across the three networks, involving cholinergic, histaminergic, glutamatergic, noradrenergic, and opioid systems. Cellular decoding showed relatively selective associations of the structural and task-based networks with glial cells and excitatory neurons, whereas the resting-state network exhibited broader associations with glial cells and multiple excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Cognitive decoding linked structural and task-based networks to sensorimotor processing and the resting-state network to memory-related functions. Our findings reconcile heterogeneous neuroimaging results and reveal neurobiological substrates of ID from a network perspective, providing a promising biomarker and paving the way for circuit-based precision therapies of ID.

item.title: ADHDeepNet: An Explainable Framework for EEG-Based ADHD Detection From Raw Signals.
item.description:
Biomedical physics & engineering express
Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a common brain disorder in children that can persist into adulthood, affecting social, academic, and career life. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing these impacts on patients and the healthcare system but is often labor-intensive and time-consuming. This paper presents a novel method to improve ADHD diagnosis precision and timeliness by leveraging Deep Learning (DL) approaches and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals. We introduce ADHDeepNet, a deep learning model that utilizes comprehensive temporal-spatial characterization, attention modules, and explainability techniques optimized for EEG signals. ADHDeepNet integrates feature extraction and refinement processes to enhance ADHD diagnosis. The model was trained and validated on a dataset of 121 participants (61 ADHD, 60 Healthy Controls), employing nested cross-validation for robust performance. The proposed two-stage methodology uses a 10-fold cross-subject validation strategy. Initially, each iteration optimizes the model's hyper-parameters with inner 2-fold cross-validation. Then, Additive Gaussian Noise (AGN) with various standard deviations and magnification levels is applied for data augmentation. ADHDeepNet achieved 100% sensitivity and 99.17% accuracy in classifying ADHD/HC subjects. To clarify model explainability and identify key brain regions and frequency bands for ADHD diagnosis, we analyzed the learned weights and activation patterns of the model's primary layers. Additionally, t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) visualized high-dimensional data, aiding in interpreting the model's decisions. This study highlights the potential of deep learning and EEG in enhancing ADHD diagnosis accuracy and efficiency.
